hypotheses.title: Registry onlyVaultMaintainer modifier uses AND instead of OR
hypotheses.description: The `onlyVaultMaintainer` modifier checks `msg.sender != vaults[_vaultId].maintainer || hasRole(EMERGENCY_ROLE, msg.sender) == false`, which reverts unless the caller is BOTH the vault maintainer AND holds EMERGENCY_ROLE. This is a logic inversion (should be `&&` with `== false` on the first clause, or `||` with `== true` on the second). The same bug exists in `onlyVaultMaintainerWithoutTimeLock` and `onlyVaultGoverner`. As a result, the intended maintainer/governer cannot call these functions unless they also hold the emergency role, and conversely the check is effectively broken.
hypotheses.attackPath: An untrusted actor cannot directly exploit this to gain access (it is over-restrictive, not under-restrictive), but it locks out legitimate maintainers/governers from `addConnector`, `updateConnectorTrustedTokens`, `removeTrustedPosition`, `addTrustedPosition`, and `changeVaultAddresses`. If the emergency role holder is a different address, the maintainer cannot perform critical configuration, and if the emergency role is compromised or removed, the vault becomes unconfigurable.
hypotheses.impact: Frozen configuration: connectors cannot be added/removed, trusted tokens cannot be updated, trusted positions cannot be added/removed, and vault addresses cannot be changed. This can brick the vault's ability to onboard new strategies or respond to incidents.
hypotheses.recommendation: Change the modifiers to `if (msg.sender != vaults[_vaultId].maintainer && hasRole(EMERGENCY_ROLE, msg.sender) == false) revert UnauthorizedAccess();` (and similarly for the other two modifiers).

hypotheses.title: Morpho TVL double-counts borrow amount in position value
hypotheses.description: `_getPositionTVL()` computes `tvl = supplyAmount + borrowAmount + convertCToL(collateral)`. For a Morpho position, `supplyAmount` is the supplied loan token (asset), `borrowAmount` is the borrowed loan token (liability), and `collateral` is the collateral token. Adding `borrowAmount` to the TVL treats the debt as an asset, inflating the vault's TVL by the borrowed amount. The correct net value should be `supplyAmount - borrowAmount + collateralValue`.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Manager opens a Morpho position with supply and borrow. 2) `_getPositionTVL()` returns an inflated TVL. 3) `totalAssets()` in AccountingManager uses this inflated TVL. 4) Share price is overstated, allowing depositors to mint shares at an inflated price and withdraw more base tokens than the vault actually holds.
hypotheses.impact: Vault TVL is overstated, share price is inflated, and the vault can become insolvent as withdrawals exceed real assets.
hypotheses.recommendation: Subtract `borrowAmount` instead of adding it: `tvl = supplyAmount - borrowAmount + convertCToL(...)`.

hypotheses.title: AccountingManager.burnShares is callable by anyone to burn their own shares
hypotheses.description: `burnShares(uint256 amount)` has no access modifier and calls `_burn(msg.sender, amount)`. Any external caller can burn their own shares at any time. While burning one's own shares is not directly a theft, it bypasses the withdraw queue and the `withdrawRequestsByAddress` accounting, and it can be used to manipulate share price / TVL accounting (e.g., to grief other depositors or to reset `withdrawRequestsByAddress` state). It also allows a user with a pending withdraw request to burn shares that are still reserved, corrupting the `withdrawRequestsByAddress` invariant checked in `_update`.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1. Attacker deposits and receives shares. 2. Attacker calls `burnShares(amount)` directly, bypassing `withdraw()` and the queue. 3. If the attacker also has a pending withdraw request, `withdrawRequestsByAddress[attacker]` remains non-zero while `balanceOf(attacker)` is reduced, causing `_update` to revert on any future transfer and potentially locking the attacker's remaining shares. 4. More generally, arbitrary burns change `totalSupply()` and thus `previewDeposit`/`previewRedeem` for all users.
hypotheses.impact: Wrong accounting of shares and TVL; potential griefing of other depositors via share-price manipulation; possible lock of the attacker's own remaining balance due to stale `withdrawRequestsByAddress`.
hypotheses.recommendation: Restrict `burnShares` to `onlyManager` or remove it entirely, or require that the caller has no pending withdraw request and route burns through the withdraw flow.

hypotheses.title: First-depositor share inflation via direct baseToken donation
hypotheses.description: `totalAssets()` returns `TVL()` which includes `baseToken.balanceOf(address(this)) - depositQueue.totalAWFDeposit`. Shares are computed via `previewDeposit` at calculation time. An attacker can deposit 1 wei first (getting 1 share), then transfer a large amount of baseToken directly to the contract (not via deposit()), inflating TVL and thus the share price. Subsequent depositors' `previewDeposit` returns 0 shares due to rounding, and their funds are captured by the attacker.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker deposits 1 wei → 1 share; 2) Attacker transfers e.g. 1e18 baseToken directly to AccountingManager; 3) Victim deposits 1e18-1 → previewDeposit returns 0 shares (rounding down); 4) Victim's funds are added to TVL; 5) Attacker redeems 1 share for ~2e18.
hypotheses.impact: Victim loses entire deposit; attacker steals funds via rounding.
hypotheses.recommendation: Use virtual shares/assets (OZ ERC4626 offset) or require minimum shares minted, and exclude direct donations from TVL.

hypotheses.title: Chainlink oracle missing round completeness and sequencer checks
hypotheses.description: The function reads `latestRoundData()` but only validates `updatedAt` against `chainlinkPriceAgeThreshold` and `price > 0`. It ignores `answeredInRound` (round completeness) and `startedAt`, and there is no L2 sequencer uptime feed check. On L2 deployments (Base is referenced in test addresses) a stale-but-recent price can be returned during sequencer downtime, and an incomplete round can return a price from a previous round.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker waits for an L2 sequencer outage or a Chainlink round that has not been finalized. 2) During the window, `latestRoundData()` returns a stale/incomplete price that still passes the age check. 3) Attacker calls deposit/withdraw or triggers TVL-dependent logic (e.g., `calculateDepositShares`, `calculateWithdrawShares`, `recordProfitForFee`) at the manipulated price. 4) Attacker mints shares cheaply or redeems at inflated value.
hypotheses.impact: Wrong share pricing, theft of vault assets via mispriced deposits/withdrawals, incorrect fee accounting.
hypotheses.recommendation: Validate `answeredInRound >= roundId`, `startedAt != 0`, and add an L2 sequencer uptime feed check with a grace period before accepting prices.

hypotheses.title: Pendle LP/PT oracle uses short TWAP duration of 10 seconds
hypotheses.description: `_getPositionTVL` calls `IPMarket(market).getLpToAssetRate(10)` and `getPtToAssetRate(10)` with a 10-second TWAP duration. A 10-second window is far too short to resist manipulation, especially on Pendle markets where liquidity can be thin. An attacker can move the market price and have the vault's TVL reflect the manipulated rate.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker flash-loans or uses capital to swap in the Pendle market, moving the implied rate. 2) Within the same block or next block, attacker triggers a vault action that reads `_getPositionTVL` (e.g., deposit/withdraw calculation, profit recording). 3) The 10s TWAP captures the manipulated rate. 4) Attacker profits from mispriced shares.
hypotheses.impact: Incorrect TVL, mispriced share issuance/redemption, potential theft of vault funds.
hypotheses.recommendation: Use a materially longer TWAP duration (e.g., 15–30 minutes) and validate that the market's observation cardinality supports it.

hypotheses.title: BalancerFlashLoan.makeFlashLoan is callable by anyone and sets caller to msg.sender
hypotheses.description: `makeFlashLoan` has no access modifier. It sets `caller = msg.sender` and then calls `vault.flashLoan(this, tokens, amounts, userData)`. In `receiveFlashLoan`, the code checks `if (!(caller == keeperContract)) revert Unauthorized(caller);` where `keeperContract` is read from the registry for the `vaultId` decoded from `userData`. An attacker can call `makeFlashLoan` with a `userData` that encodes a `vaultId` whose `keeperContract` equals the attacker's address (if the attacker is a keeper for some vault) or, more importantly, the attacker can pass arbitrary `userData` and the check only verifies `caller == keeperContract` for the decoded `vaultId`. If the attacker is not a keeper, the check reverts, but the attacker can still trigger the flash loan and cause the vault to send tokens to `receiver` if `receiver` is an active connector — the `caller` check is the only gate, and it is set to `msg.sender` (the attacker), so the attacker must be the keeper. However, the real issue is that `makeFlashLoan` is not restricted to the keeper at the entry point; the check is deferred to `receiveFlashLoan` and depends on `userData` decoding. An attacker who is a keeper for ANY vault can pass a different `vaultId` in `userData` and have the check pass if that vault's keeper is also the attacker.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1. Attacker is a keeper for vault A (or controls a keeper). 2. Attacker calls `makeFlashLoan` with `userData` encoding vault B's `vaultId` where the keeper is also the attacker (or where the attacker can satisfy the check). 3. `receiveFlashLoan` decodes vault B's `vaultId`, reads vault B's `keeperContract`, and if it equals `caller` (the attacker), proceeds. 4. The attacker can then direct `destinationConnector` calls and `receiver` to drain vault B's tokens via `sendTokensToTrustedAddress`.
hypotheses.impact: Unauthorized flash loans against any vault whose keeper is the attacker; potential theft of vault funds via arbitrary `destinationConnector` calls and `receiver` transfers.
hypotheses.recommendation: Add an `onlyKeeper`-style check at the entry point of `makeFlashLoan` (verify `msg.sender` is the keeper for the `vaultId` encoded in `userData` before calling `vault.flashLoan`), and validate `receiver` and `destinationConnector` against the registry before executing calls.

hypotheses.title: LifiImplementation.performSwapAction trusts caller-supplied `from` for token pull
hypotheses.description: `performSwapAction` is `onlyHandler` (the SwapAndBridgeHandler). It calls `_forward` which invokes `ITokenTransferCallBack(from).sendTokensToTrustedAddress(...)` where `from` is `_request.from` supplied by the caller of the swap handler. The swap handler is `onlyEligibleUser`, but any eligible user (e.g. a connector) can craft a `SwapRequest` with `from` set to an arbitrary address that implements `sendTokensToTrustedAddress` and returns success without actually transferring tokens. `verifySwapData` only checks that the LiFi calldata's `from` matches `_request.from`, not that `_request.from` is the actual caller or a trusted contract. The result is that the LiFi call is executed with `msg.value` and any allowance set on `token` for `lifi`, but the input tokens may never have been received, allowing the caller to drain value or execute arbitrary LiFi calls with the handler's context.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker becomes an eligible user (or is a connector). 2) Attacker deploys a contract `Fake` implementing `sendTokensToTrustedAddress` that returns without transferring. 3) Attacker calls `SwapAndBridgeHandler.executeSwap` with `_request.from = Fake`, `_request.inputToken = someToken`, `_request.data` = valid LiFi generic swap calldata with `from = Fake`. 4) `verifySwapData` passes because LiFi calldata `from` matches `Fake`. 5) `_forward` calls `Fake.sendTokensToTrustedAddress` which does nothing, then calls `lifi.call{value: msg.value}(data)`. 6) LiFi executes the swap using whatever balance/allowance the handler has, potentially draining tokens the handler holds or executing unintended swaps.
hypotheses.impact: Theft of tokens held by the handler or misuse of allowances; arbitrary LiFi calls executed with handler privileges.
hypotheses.recommendation: Require `_request.from == msg.sender` (or a trusted connector) and verify the actual token balance delta on the handler before forwarding to LiFi.

hypotheses.title: Withdraw fee taken from user but not accounted in totalWithdrawnAmount
hypotheses.description: In executeWithdraw, `processedBaseTokenAmount += data.amount` (the pre-fee amount) is added to `totalWithdrawnAmount`, but the user only receives `baseTokenAmount - feeAmount`. The fee is transferred to `withdrawFeeReceiver` separately. Since `getProfit()` uses `tvl + totalWithdrawnAmount - totalDepositedAmount`, the fee amount is double-counted: it is both removed from the vault (transferred to fee receiver) and added to totalWithdrawnAmount, inflating profit and thus performance fees.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) User withdraws; 2) fee is deducted and sent to receiver; 3) totalWithdrawnAmount is incremented by the full pre-fee amount; 4) getProfit() overstates profit by the fee amount; 5) strategy manager calls recordProfitForFee() and collectPerformanceFees() to mint extra shares backed by nothing.
hypotheses.impact: Inflated profit accounting → excess performance fee shares minted → dilution of all shareholders and eventual insolvency of the vault's share backing.
hypotheses.recommendation: Add only the net amount actually paid out (baseTokenAmount after fee) to totalWithdrawnAmount, or track fees separately.

hypotheses.title: UniswapValueOracle uses spot slot0-derived TWAP with no cardinality check
hypotheses.description: The oracle calls `IUniswapV3Pool(pool).observe(secondsAgos)` with a fixed `period` (default 1800s) but never verifies that the pool's `observationCardinality` is large enough to cover that period. If the pool has been recently created or cardinality was not increased, `observe` reverts or returns a window shorter than requested, and the resulting TWAP can be trivially manipulated by an attacker who controls the pool's price over the available window.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker identifies a pool used by the vault whose observation cardinality is small (or grows it themselves by trading). 2) Attacker performs a large swap to move the tick, then triggers a vault action that calls `getValue` within the same short window. 3) The TWAP over the truncated window reflects the manipulated price. 4) Attacker deposits/withdraws at the wrong price.
hypotheses.impact: Vault TVL mispricing, share inflation/deflation, loss of funds to attacker.
hypotheses.recommendation: Require `observationCardinality >= required` for the configured period, or use `OracleLibrary.consult` with a check that the oldest observation covers `period`.

hypotheses.title: executeWithdraw reads totalCBAmountFullfilled after it is zeroed
hypotheses.description: In `fulfillCurrentWithdrawGroup()`, `currentWithdrawGroup.totalCBAmount` is set to 0 after being copied into `totalCBAmountFullfilled`. In `executeWithdraw()`, the per-user payout is computed as `data.amount * currentWithdrawGroup.totalABAmount / currentWithdrawGroup.totalCBAmountFullfilled`. Because `totalCBAmountFullfilled` is set to the pre-zero value this is fine on the first call, but the group is deleted only when `lastId == firstTemp`. If `executeWithdraw` is called with `maxIterations` smaller than the group size, the group persists and subsequent calls still divide by the same `totalCBAmountFullfilled`, which is correct — but the real issue is that `totalABAmount` is computed from `availableAssets` at fulfill time, while `totalCBAmountFullfilled` is the full requested amount. If `availableAssets < totalCBAmount`, users are paid pro-rata, but `processedBaseTokenAmount` is incremented by `data.amount` (the requested amount, not the paid amount), corrupting `totalWithdrawnAmount` and thus `getProfit()`.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1. Attacker deposits, waits for calculation, then withdraws a large share. 2. Manager fulfills the group when `availableAssets < totalCBAmount` (partial fill). 3. `executeWithdraw` pays each user `data.amount * totalABAmount / totalCBAmountFullfilled` (less than `data.amount`) but adds the full `data.amount` to `totalWithdrawnAmount`. 4. `getProfit()` = `TVL + totalWithdrawnAmount - totalDepositedAmount` is inflated, so `recordProfitForFee` mints excess performance-fee shares to the fee receiver, diluting all holders.
hypotheses.impact: Wrong accounting of `totalWithdrawnAmount` inflates reported profit, minting unearned performance-fee shares and diluting honest depositors.
hypotheses.recommendation: Increment `totalWithdrawnAmount` by the actual `baseTokenAmount` paid (post-fee) rather than `data.amount`, or track the pro-rata paid amount separately.

hypotheses.title: Anyone can freeze the withdraw group by calling checkIfTVLHasDroped
hypotheses.description: `checkIfTVLHasDroped()` is public and resets `preformanceFeeSharesWaitingForDistribution` and `profitStoredTime` whenever `getProfit() < storedProfitForFee`. Because `getProfit()` depends on `TVL()` which reads live oracle prices and connector balances, any external actor can call this at a moment when TVL dips (e.g. via a small swap that moves a Uniswap TWAP, or by front-running a price move) to wipe the pending performance fee state. More importantly, the same public entrypoint can be spammed to keep resetting `profitStoredTime`, permanently preventing `collectPerformanceFees()` from ever succeeding (it requires `block.timestamp - profitStoredTime` between 12h and 48h).
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker observes `storedProfitForFee > 0` and `profitStoredTime` set. 2) Attacker triggers a tiny price move (or waits for natural volatility) so `getProfit() < storedProfitForFee`. 3) Attacker calls `checkIfTVLHasDroped()` repeatedly, resetting `profitStoredTime = 0` and `preformanceFeeSharesWaitingForDistribution = 0`. 4) `collectPerformanceFees()` can never satisfy its time window.
hypotheses.impact: Performance fee shares are permanently unclaimable; protocol fee accounting is corrupted; strategy manager loses earned fees.
hypotheses.recommendation: Restrict `checkIfTVLHasDroped()` to a trusted role, or only allow it to zero the pending shares without resetting `profitStoredTime` to 0.

hypotheses.title: Performance fee shares minted without burning on TVL drop
hypotheses.description: `recordProfitForFee()` mints `preformanceFeeSharesWaitingForDistribution` shares to `address(this)` (via `previewDeposit`) but does not actually mint them; the shares are only minted later in `collectPerformanceFees()`. When TVL drops, `checkIfTVLHasDroped()` sets `preformanceFeeSharesWaitingForDistribution = 0` and `profitStoredTime = 0`, but the previously "reserved" shares were never minted, so no burn is needed. However, `totalProfitCalculated` is not reset, and the manager can call `recordProfitForFee()` again after the drop to re-arm the fee on the same profit once TVL recovers, effectively double-counting profit that was already accounted for. The check `if (storedProfitForFee < totalProfitCalculated) return;` only guards against lower profit, not against re-arming after a reset.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Manager records profit P1, `totalProfitCalculated` stays at old value. 2) TVL drops, `checkIfTVLHasDroped()` zeroes pending shares but leaves `totalProfitCalculated` unchanged. 3) TVL recovers to P1 again. 4) Manager calls `recordProfitForFee()` again; since `storedProfitForFee >= totalProfitCalculated`, new fee shares are computed on `(P1 - totalProfitCalculated)` which is the same profit already charged. 5) Manager collects fees twice on the same profit.
hypotheses.impact: Performance fee is charged multiple times on the same profit, diluting LPs and transferring value to the fee receiver.
hypotheses.recommendation: On TVL drop, also reset `totalProfitCalculated` to the current profit (or track a high-water mark) so the same profit cannot be re-charged.

hypotheses.title: PendleConnector.isMarketEmpty ignores Penpie deposits
hypotheses.description: `isMarketEmpty` checks `_SY.balanceOf(address(this)) == 0 && _PT.balanceOf(address(this)) == 0 && _YT.balanceOf(address(this)) == 0 && market.balanceOf(address(this)) == 0`. It does NOT check `pendleMarketDepositHelper.balance(market, address(this))`, which is the LP balance deposited into Penpie. If LP tokens are deposited into Penpie via `depositIntoPenpie`, `market.balanceOf(address(this))` is 0 (tokens are in Penpie), so `isMarketEmpty` returns true even though the position is not empty. This is called in `decreasePosition` to decide whether to remove the holding position from the registry.
hypotheses.attackPath: Manager calls `depositIntoPenpie(market, amount)` to deposit LP into Penpie. Then calls `decreasePosition(market, 0, true)` with `_amount = 0` (or a small amount that doesn't empty the position). `isMarketEmpty` returns true because `market.balanceOf(address(this)) == 0`, so the holding position is removed from the registry even though Penpie still holds LP. The position's TVL is no longer counted, understating the vault's assets.
hypotheses.impact: Registry holding position removed while assets remain in Penpie, causing TVL understatement and potential loss of accounting for those assets.
hypotheses.recommendation: Include `pendleMarketDepositHelper.balance(market, address(this)) == 0` in the `isMarketEmpty` check.

hypotheses.title: Pendle getYTValue uses static router spot quote for TVL
hypotheses.description: `getYTValue` calls `staticRouter.swapExactYtForSyStatic(market, balance)` which returns a spot quote based on current market state, not a TWAP. This value is added directly into `_getPositionTVL` for YT holdings. An attacker can manipulate the Pendle market state (via a swap) and have the vault's TVL reflect the manipulated YT value.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker swaps in the Pendle market to skew the YT/SY rate. 2) Attacker triggers a vault action that reads `_getPositionTVL` for the Pendle position. 3) The inflated/deflated YT value flows into TVL. 4) Attacker deposits or withdraws at the wrong price.
hypotheses.impact: Mispriced shares, incorrect profit/fee accounting, potential fund loss.
hypotheses.recommendation: Use a TWAP-based YT valuation (e.g., derive from `getPtToAssetRate` with a long duration) instead of the static spot quote.

hypotheses.title: BalancerFlashLoan.receiveFlashLoan trusts userData for vaultId and receiver without binding to caller
hypotheses.description: `makeFlashLoan` sets `caller = msg.sender` and then calls `vault.flashLoan`. In `receiveFlashLoan`, the code decodes `userData` to obtain `vaultId`, `receiver`, `destinationConnector`, `callingData`, `gas`. It then checks `caller == keeperContract` for the decoded `vaultId`. However, `caller` is set to `msg.sender` of `makeFlashLoan`, and the check is against the keeper of the *decoded* vaultId. An attacker who is a keeper of any vault can call `makeFlashLoan` with `userData` encoding a *different* vaultId whose keeper is also the attacker (or whose keeper check passes), and set `receiver` to an arbitrary active connector of that vault. The `destinationConnector` calls are executed with `gas[i]` and arbitrary `callingData`, and the receiver is instructed to send tokens back via `sendTokensToTrustedAddress`. Because `receiver` is only checked to be an active connector of the decoded vaultId, and `destinationConnector` calls are unrestricted, an attacker can invoke arbitrary functions on any contract via the flash loan, and the repayment logic relies on the receiver returning tokens.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker is a keeper of vault A. 2) Attacker calls `makeFlashLoan` with `userData` encoding `vaultId = A`, `receiver = someActiveConnectorOfA`, `destinationConnector = [attackerControlledContract]`, `callingData = [arbitraryCall]`, `gas = [large]`. 3) `receiveFlashLoan` checks `caller == keeperContract` for vault A (passes). 4) Tokens are sent to `receiver`, then `destinationConnector[i].call{gas: gas[i]}(callingData[i])` executes arbitrary code. 5) Attacker's contract can re-enter or manipulate state, and the repayment step calls `receiver.sendTokensToTrustedAddress` which may be manipulated.
hypotheses.impact: Arbitrary external calls with flash-loaned funds; potential theft or state manipulation.
hypotheses.recommendation: Bind `userData` to the caller by hashing it in `makeFlashLoan` and verifying in `receiveFlashLoan`, and restrict `destinationConnector` to active connectors of the same vault.

hypotheses.title: Deposit limit check uses TVL before pending deposits are counted
hypotheses.description: `deposit()` checks `TVL() > depositLimitTotalAmount` before adding the new deposit to the queue. `TVL()` excludes `depositQueue.totalAWFDeposit` (pending deposits), so a user can deposit up to `depositLimitPerTransaction` repeatedly while TVL is below the limit, even though the sum of pending deposits plus TVL exceeds `depositLimitTotalAmount`. The limit is only enforced against realized TVL, not against committed deposits.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) TVL is just below `depositLimitTotalAmount`. 2) Attacker submits many deposits each at `depositLimitPerTransaction`. 3) Each deposit passes the TVL check because pending deposits are not counted. 4) Total committed deposits exceed the intended cap.
hypotheses.impact: Deposit cap is bypassed, allowing more capital than intended into the vault, potentially exceeding risk limits.
hypotheses.recommendation: Include `depositQueue.totalAWFDeposit` in the TVL check, or check `TVL() + amount > depositLimitTotalAmount`.

hypotheses.title: NoyaFeeReceiver.withdrawShares and burnShares are onlyOwner but owner can be any address
hypotheses.description: `NoyaFeeReceiver` is `Ownable` and its `withdrawShares`/`burnShares` are `onlyOwner`. The owner is set to `msg.sender` at construction. If the fee receiver is deployed by a non-governance address (e.g., a keeper or an EOA), that address can call `AccountingManager.withdraw(amount, receiver)` on behalf of the fee receiver, draining the fee receiver's shares to `receiver`. Since `AccountingManager.withdraw` uses `msg.sender` as the share owner, the fee receiver's shares are used. There is no check that the caller is the vault's governance or that `receiver` is the intended fee recipient.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1. If the fee receiver's owner is an untrusted EOA (e.g., a compromised deployer key or a keeper), that owner calls `withdrawShares(amount)`. 2. `AccountingManager.withdraw` is invoked with `msg.sender == NoyaFeeReceiver`, so the fee receiver's shares are queued for withdrawal to `receiver`. 3. The owner can set `receiver` to any address at construction, so fees can be redirected.
hypotheses.impact: Theft of accumulated management/performance/withdraw fees from the vault's fee receiver.
hypotheses.recommendation: Make `NoyaFeeReceiver` owner a governance-controlled address (e.g., the vault's maintainer or a timelock) and/or restrict `withdrawShares`/`burnShares` to the vault's governance roles via the registry.

hypotheses.title: SwapAndBridgeHandler.executeSwap minAmount can be zero when checkForSlippage is false
hypotheses.description: `executeSwap` is `onlyEligibleUser` and `onlyExistingRoute`. The slippage check is only applied when `_swapRequest.checkForSlippage` is true and `_swapRequest.minAmount == 0`. If `checkForSlippage` is false, `minAmount` is passed through to the implementation without any validation. An eligible user (e.g., a connector or a compromised eligible address) can set `checkForSlippage = false` and `minAmount = 0`, causing the swap to execute with no slippage protection. While `onlyEligibleUser` restricts callers, the eligible user set is managed by `addEligibleUser` (maintainer/emergency), and a compromised eligible user can drain value via sandwich attacks.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1. Attacker gains eligibility (e.g., via a compromised eligible user or by being added). 2. Attacker calls `executeSwap` with `checkForSlippage = false` and `minAmount = 0`. 3. The swap executes with no minimum output, allowing MEV bots to sandwich the trade. 4. The vault loses value on the swap.
hypotheses.impact: Loss of funds via sandwich/MEV attacks on swaps executed without slippage protection.
hypotheses.recommendation: Always enforce a non-zero `minAmount` (or compute it from the oracle) regardless of `checkForSlippage`, or require `checkForSlippage == true` for all swaps.

hypotheses.title: recordProfitForFee mints shares based on stale totalProfitCalculated
hypotheses.description: `preformanceFeeSharesWaitingForDistribution = previewDeposit(((storedProfitForFee - totalProfitCalculated) * performanceFee) / FEE_PRECISION)`. `previewDeposit` uses current TVL which already includes the profit. This means the fee shares are computed at the post-profit share price, undercounting the fee (fee should be computed on profit before dilution). Additionally, if `storedProfitForFee < totalProfitCalculated`, the function returns early without resetting `preformanceFeeSharesWaitingForDistribution`, leaving stale pending fee shares.
hypotheses.attackPath: Manager calls recordProfitForFee when profit is lower than previously calculated; stale `preformanceFeeSharesWaitingForDistribution` remains and can be collected later when profit recovers, overpaying fees.
hypotheses.impact: Incorrect fee distribution; either over- or under-payment of performance fees.
hypotheses.recommendation: Reset `preformanceFeeSharesWaitingForDistribution = 0` in the early-return branch, and compute fee shares using pre-profit share price.

hypotheses.title: ChainlinkOracleConnector inverse price uses wrong decimals source
hypotheses.description: When `isPrimaryInverse` is true, `decimalsSource = baseToken`. But the inverse formula `(amountIn * sourceTokenUnit) / uintprice` uses `sourceTokenUnit` derived from `decimalsSource`. For inverse feeds, the price feed gives baseToken/asset, so the correct unit is the asset's decimals, not the base token's. This produces wrong values when asset and baseToken have different decimals.
hypotheses.attackPath: Any user triggering a valuation (e.g., via deposit/withdraw) where the oracle is configured inversely and decimals differ gets a mispriced value, enabling arbitrage or under/over-collateralization.
hypotheses.impact: Incorrect TVL → wrong share price → theft via deposit/withdraw arbitrage.
hypotheses.recommendation: For inverse feeds, use the asset's decimals as the source token unit.

hypotheses.title: SwapHandler slippage check uses oracle value, not actual swap output
hypotheses.description: When `checkForSlippage` is true and `minAmount == 0`, the handler computes `minAmount` from `valueOracle.getValue(inputToken, outputToken, amount)` and applies a slippage tolerance. This means the minimum-out is derived from the same oracle that may itself be manipulable, and the actual swap output is never compared against a user-supplied minimum. If the oracle is wrong or manipulated, the swap can execute at a much worse rate than intended.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker manipulates the oracle used by `valueOracle` (e.g., Uniswap TWAP pool). 2) Attacker triggers a vault swap via `swapHoldings` with `checkForSlippage=true` and `minAmount=0`. 3) The computed `minAmount` is based on the manipulated price, allowing the swap to execute at an unfavorable rate. 4) Attacker captures the difference via their own liquidity.
hypotheses.impact: Vault loses value on swaps, funds extracted by attacker.
hypotheses.recommendation: Require callers to supply an explicit `minAmount` derived from a trusted source, or use a robust oracle with manipulation resistance and validate the actual output against it.

hypotheses.title: deposit() checks TVL limit after transferring tokens in
hypotheses.description: `deposit()` performs `baseToken.safeTransferFrom(msg.sender, address(this), amount)` before checking `amount > depositLimitPerTransaction` and `TVL() > depositLimitTotalAmount`. If either check reverts, the whole transaction reverts, so funds are not lost — but the ordering means the TVL check uses the post-transfer balance, so a user can push TVL over the limit and the check reverts only after the transfer. More importantly, `TVL()` includes `baseToken.balanceOf(address(this))`, so the just-transferred amount is counted, making the limit check stricter than intended and allowing a griefer to temporarily block deposits by front-running with a large deposit that reverts.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1. Attacker observes a pending deposit. 2. Attacker front-runs with a deposit that pushes `TVL()` above `depositLimitTotalAmount`. 3. Victim's deposit reverts because the check runs after the transfer and includes the attacker's amount. 4. Attacker's own deposit also reverts, but the victim's legitimate deposit is blocked.
hypotheses.impact: Denial of service on deposits; griefing of legitimate users.
hypotheses.recommendation: Perform the limit checks before `safeTransferFrom`, or compute TVL excluding the incoming amount.

hypotheses.title: BalancerFlashLoan caller reset allows reentrant misuse
hypotheses.description: `makeFlashLoan` sets `caller = msg.sender`, calls `vault.flashLoan(...)`, then resets `caller = address(0)`. During `receiveFlashLoan`, the contract executes arbitrary `callingData` on `destinationConnector[i]` via low-level `call`. If any of those calls reenters `makeFlashLoan`, `caller` is overwritten with the new `msg.sender` (which must be the keeper contract to pass the check). Since `caller` is a single storage slot shared across the whole flow, a nested flash loan can overwrite the outer `caller`, and when the inner call returns, the outer `receiveFlashLoan` continues with the inner `caller` value — but the check already passed. More critically, the reset to `address(0)` at the end of the inner call wipes the outer `caller`, so the outer `receiveFlashLoan`'s subsequent iterations see `caller == address(0)` and revert, or worse, if the check is skipped, unauthorized execution.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1. Keeper initiates a flash loan. 2. During `receiveFlashLoan`, a destination connector call reenters `makeFlashLoan` (keeper is msg.sender). 3. Inner call sets `caller = keeper`, executes, then resets `caller = address(0)`. 4. Outer `receiveFlashLoan` continues; if it re-checks `caller`, it now sees `address(0)` and reverts, or if the check is only at the top, the outer flow proceeds with corrupted state.
hypotheses.impact: Flash loan flow can be disrupted or, if the check is bypassed, unauthorized connectors can be invoked.
hypotheses.recommendation: Use a transient/local variable for `caller` instead of storage, or use a reentrancy guard on `makeFlashLoan`.

hypotheses.title: Unbounded withdraw queue growth blocks executeWithdraw via gas
hypotheses.description: `withdraw()` appends to `withdrawQueue.queue` with no cap on `withdrawQueue.last`. `executeWithdraw()` iterates from `withdrawQueue.first` to `currentWithdrawGroup.lastId` with a caller-supplied `maxIterations`, but `calculateWithdrawShares()` and `startCurrentWithdrawGroup()` must process the entire middle range before a group can be fulfilled. An attacker can submit many tiny withdraw requests (1 wei of shares each) to inflate the queue, forcing managers to spend enormous gas to advance `middle`/`first`, and potentially making the queue unprocessable within block gas limits.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker acquires minimal shares. 2) Attacker calls `withdraw(1, attacker)` thousands of times across blocks. 3) `withdrawQueue.last` grows unbounded. 4) Manager calls to `calculateWithdrawShares`/`executeWithdraw` become prohibitively expensive; the withdraw group cannot be fulfilled in reasonable time.
hypotheses.impact: Withdrawals for all users are delayed or effectively frozen; funds stuck in the vault.
hypotheses.recommendation: Enforce a minimum withdraw size and/or a maximum queue length, and allow skipping/aggregating dust requests.

hypotheses.title: Withdraw fee taken from pro-rata amount can leave group underfunded
hypotheses.description: In `executeWithdraw()`, `baseTokenAmount` is computed as `data.amount * totalABAmount / totalCBAmountFullfilled`, then `withdrawFee` is subtracted and the remainder is sent to the user. The fee is transferred to `withdrawFeeReceiver` from the same pool. If `totalABAmount < totalCBAmountFullfilled` (partial fulfillment), the sum of user payouts plus fees can exceed `totalABAmount` because the fee is taken from the already-reduced pro-rata amount, not from the full `data.amount`. This can drain the contract's base token balance below what is needed for remaining withdrawers in the same group.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) A withdraw group is partially fulfilled (`totalABAmount < totalCBAmountFullfilled`). 2) Users execute withdrawals; each payout is `data.amount * totalABAmount / totalCBAmountFullfilled` minus fee. 3) The fee is sent out in addition to the reduced payout. 4) The contract's base token balance is depleted faster than the pro-rata accounting assumes, leaving later withdrawers in the group unable to be paid.
hypotheses.impact: Later withdrawers in the same group receive less than their pro-rata share or the transaction reverts, freezing funds.
hypotheses.recommendation: Compute the fee on the full `data.amount` before applying the pro-rata scaling, or deduct the fee from `totalABAmount` before distributing.

hypotheses.title: Silo TVL uses raw token balances ignoring debt sign
hypotheses.description: `_getPositionTVL()` computes `totalDepositAmount` from collateral token balances and `totalBAmount` from debt token balances, then returns `totalDepositAmount - totalBAmount`. However, `borrowAmount` is read from `IERC20(assetsS[i].debtToken).balanceOf(address(this))`, which is the debt token balance (a liability). The subtraction is correct in sign, but the function does not account for accrued interest on the debt (the debt token balance is a share balance, not the underlying amount). The TVL is therefore understated relative to the actual debt, overstating the vault's net value.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Manager opens a Silo position with borrow. 2) Interest accrues on the debt. 3) `_getPositionTVL()` uses the raw debt token balance (shares) instead of converting to underlying amount. 4) TVL is overstated, share price is inflated, and withdrawals can exceed real assets.
hypotheses.impact: Vault TVL is overstated, leading to inflated share price and potential insolvency.
hypotheses.recommendation: Convert debt token shares to underlying amount using the Silo's exchange rate before subtracting.

hypotheses.title: executeWithdraw divides by totalCBAmountFullfilled which can be zero
hypotheses.description: In `executeWithdraw`, the base token amount is computed as `data.amount * currentWithdrawGroup.totalABAmount / currentWithdrawGroup.totalCBAmountFullfilled`. `totalCBAmountFullfilled` is set in `fulfillCurrentWithdrawGroup` to `currentWithdrawGroup.totalCBAmount` before it is zeroed. If `calculateWithdrawShares` was called with `maxIterations` such that no shares were processed (e.g., all requests are newer than `oldestUpdateTime`), `totalCBAmount` remains 0. Then `startCurrentWithdrawGroup` sets `lastId = withdrawQueue.middle` (unchanged), and `fulfillCurrentWithdrawGroup` sets `totalCBAmountFullfilled = 0`. If `executeWithdraw` is then called with `currentWithdrawGroup.lastId > firstTemp` (which requires `middle > first`), the division by zero reverts. More critically, if `totalCBAmountFullfilled` is 0 but `lastId > firstTemp` is false, the loop doesn't execute. The real risk: if `totalCBAmount` is 0 but `lastId > firstTemp` somehow holds (e.g., via `resetMiddle`), division by zero. Also, `fulfillCurrentWithdrawGroup` requires `amountAskedForWithdraw == currentWithdrawGroup.totalCBAmount` when `neededAssets != 0`; if `totalCBAmount` is 0 and `neededAssets` is 0, it proceeds and sets `totalCBAmountFullfilled = 0`.
hypotheses.attackPath: Manager calls `calculateWithdrawShares` when no requests are eligible (all newer than oldestUpdateTime), so `totalCBAmount` stays 0. Then `startCurrentWithdrawGroup` sets `lastId = middle`. Then `fulfillCurrentWithdrawGroup` sets `totalCBAmountFullfilled = 0`. Then `executeWithdraw` is called; if `lastId > firstTemp` (which requires `middle > first`, possible if `first` was advanced by a previous group but `middle` wasn't), the division by zero reverts, bricking withdrawals.
hypotheses.impact: Withdrawals permanently revert (DoS), freezing user funds in the withdraw queue.
hypotheses.recommendation: In `fulfillCurrentWithdrawGroup`, require `currentWithdrawGroup.totalCBAmount > 0` before setting `totalCBAmountFullfilled`, or in `executeWithdraw` guard against `totalCBAmountFullfilled == 0`.

hypotheses.title: fulfillCurrentWithdrawGroup uses stale totalCBAmount after reset
hypotheses.description: `currentWithdrawGroup.totalCBAmount` is set to 0 at the end of fulfillCurrentWithdrawGroup, but the emit uses it after resetting (emits 0). More importantly, `totalCBAmountFullfilled` is set to `totalCBAmount` before reset, and executeWithdraw divides by `totalCBAmountFullfilled`. If `totalCBAmount` is 0 (no withdraws calculated) but the group is started, division by zero occurs in executeWithdraw. Also, if `availableAssets < totalCBAmount`, `totalABAmount` is set to availableAssets, but `totalCBAmountFullfilled` remains the full amount, so users receive proportionally less — this is intended, but the emit reports 0.
hypotheses.attackPath: Manager starts withdraw group with no calculated withdraws (totalCBAmount=0), then fulfills; executeWithdraw divides by zero → DoS. Or the emit misreports.
hypotheses.impact: DoS on executeWithdraw; incorrect event data.
hypotheses.recommendation: Guard against totalCBAmountFullfilled == 0 in executeWithdraw and emit before resetting.

hypotheses.title: collectManagementFees mints shares diluting existing holders without asset backing
hypotheses.description: Management fee shares are minted to `managementFeeReceiver` based on `totalShares - currentFeeShares`. However, `currentFeeShares` only subtracts balances of fee receivers and pending performance fee shares, not shares held by the vault itself or other pending deposits. More critically, minting new shares dilutes existing holders without adding assets, and the formula uses `totalShares` which includes shares that will be minted for pending deposits (depositQueue), causing fee over- or under-calculation.
hypotheses.attackPath: Manager calls collectManagementFees repeatedly; the formula's `totalShares` includes shares not yet minted for queued deposits, so fee shares are computed on a larger base than actual circulating supply, over-minting fee shares.
hypotheses.impact: Excessive dilution of depositors; fee receiver gets more than intended.
hypotheses.recommendation: Use actual circulating supply (totalSupply minus pending deposit shares) and cap fee shares.

hypotheses.title: retrieveTokensForWithdraw trusts connector-reported amount
hypotheses.description: `retrieveTokensForWithdraw` calls `IConnector(connectorAddress).sendTokensToTrustedAddress(...)` and uses the returned `amount` to update `amountAskedForWithdraw`. The check `balanceBefore + amount > balanceAfter` only ensures the balance increased by at least `amount`, but a malicious or compromised connector (which is a trusted role, so not directly exploitable) — however, the connector calls back into `AccountingManager.sendTokensToTrustedAddress`, which transfers tokens out. A reentrant call during `sendTokensToTrustedAddress` could manipulate `amountAskedForWithdraw` before the outer loop finishes, since `amountAskedForWithdraw` is only updated after the loop.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1. A connector (trusted) is invoked. 2. During `sendTokensToTrustedAddress`, the connector reenters `AccountingManager` via a callback that reads `amountAskedForWithdraw` (still stale) and `neededAssetsForWithdraw()`. 3. The stale value allows `fulfillCurrentWithdrawGroup` to be called with an incorrect `amountAskedForWithdraw`, marking the group fulfilled prematurely.
hypotheses.impact: Withdraw group can be fulfilled with insufficient assets, causing later withdrawers to receive less than owed.
hypotheses.recommendation: Update `amountAskedForWithdraw` incrementally inside the loop, or add a reentrancy guard on the callback path.

hypotheses.title: deposit() reverts after transferFrom when amount exceeds per-tx limit
hypotheses.category: Denial of Service / Revert on Zero Transfer
hypotheses.description: In `deposit()`, `baseToken.safeTransferFrom(msg.sender, address(this), amount)` is executed before the `amount > depositLimitPerTransaction` check. If the check reverts, the whole transaction reverts, so the transfer is rolled back — but the ordering means any integration that pre-approves and relies on partial success will fail. More critically, the `TVL() > depositLimitTotalAmount` check uses `TVL()` which includes `baseToken.balanceOf(address(this)) - depositQueue.totalAWFDeposit`; a large pending deposit queue can push TVL over the limit and block all new deposits, including small ones, until the queue is processed.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker deposits up to the per-tx limit repeatedly to inflate `depositQueue.totalAWFDeposit` and `TVL()`. 2) Once `TVL() > depositLimitTotalAmount`, all subsequent `deposit()` calls revert. 3) Legitimate users cannot deposit until the manager processes the queue.
hypotheses.impact: Deposits frozen for all users; griefing vector with no cost beyond gas.
hypotheses.recommendation: Move the limit checks before `safeTransferFrom`, and base the total-limit check on committed (not pending) deposits.

hypotheses.title: BalancerFlashLoan.receiveFlashLoan trusts caller set by anyone
hypotheses.description: `makeFlashLoan()` sets `caller = msg.sender` and then calls `vault.flashLoan`. In `receiveFlashLoan`, the check is `if (!(caller == keeperContract)) revert Unauthorized(caller)`. Since `caller` is set to `msg.sender` of `makeFlashLoan`, any address can call `makeFlashLoan` and set `caller` to itself; the subsequent `receiveFlashLoan` will revert because `caller != keeperContract`. This is a griefing vector: an attacker can call `makeFlashLoan` with arbitrary `userData` and cause the Balancer vault to invoke `receiveFlashLoan`, which reverts, wasting gas and potentially disrupting Balancer's flash loan accounting if the vault does not handle reverts gracefully. More importantly, if `keeperContract` is ever set to an attacker-controlled address (not in scope), the check is bypassed.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker calls `makeFlashLoan(tokens, amounts, maliciousUserData)`. 2) `caller` is set to attacker. 3) Balancer vault calls `receiveFlashLoan`. 4) Check `caller == keeperContract` fails, reverting the flash loan. 5) Repeated calls waste gas and can disrupt Balancer vault operations.
hypotheses.impact: Griefing of flash loan mechanism; potential disruption of Balancer vault.
hypotheses.recommendation: Require `msg.sender == keeperContract` in `makeFlashLoan` before setting `caller`.

hypotheses.title: NoyaValueOracle.getValue follows arbitrary priceRoutes without validating sources
hypotheses.description: `getValue` reads `priceRoutes[asset][baseToken]` and iterates through `sources`, calling `_getValue(asset, sources[i], initialValue)` and then `_getValue(quotingToken, baseToken, initialValue)`. The `sources` array is set by the maintainer via `updatePriceRoute`. If a route is misconfigured or a source oracle is malicious/compromised, the value returned can be arbitrarily manipulated. Since `AccountingManager.TVL()` and connector TVL functions rely on this oracle, a manipulated price directly affects share pricing, deposit/withdraw calculations, and fee minting. An untrusted actor cannot set routes, but if any source oracle is a contract that can be influenced (e.g., a Uniswap pool with low liquidity), the attacker can manipulate the pool to skew the reported value.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker identifies a route where a source is a Uniswap V3 pool with low liquidity. 2) Attacker performs a large swap to move the TWAP tick. 3) `getValue` returns a skewed value. 4) Attacker deposits or withdraws at the manipulated price, extracting value from the vault.
hypotheses.impact: Wrong accounting, theft via mispriced deposits/withdrawals, insolvency.
hypotheses.recommendation: Enforce minimum liquidity/TWAP duration checks on oracle sources and validate that each source returns a sane value.

hypotheses.title: Management fee minted on stale share count ignoring pending deposits
hypotheses.description: `collectManagementFees()` computes `managementFeeAmount` from `totalShares - currentFeeShares`, where `currentFeeShares` only subtracts fee-receiver balances and pending performance shares. It does not account for shares that will be minted for pending deposits in `executeDeposit()`. Since deposits are queued and only minted after `depositWaitingTime`, the management fee is charged on a share supply that excludes pending depositors, but those depositors will receive shares at the pre-fee price. The fee is therefore under-charged relative to the eventual share supply, and the manager can time `collectManagementFees()` to mint shares right before large deposits execute, diluting existing holders less than intended.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Manager observes a large pending deposit in the queue. 2) Calls `collectManagementFees()` before `executeDeposit()` mints the new shares. 3) Fee is computed on the smaller pre-deposit share supply. 4) New depositors receive shares at a price that already reflects the fee dilution, so the fee receiver gets fewer shares than if the fee had been computed after the deposit.
hypotheses.impact: Management fee under-collection; fee receiver loses value and the accounting is inconsistent with the actual share supply.
hypotheses.recommendation: Include pending deposit shares (or compute the fee on the post-deposit supply) when calculating `currentFeeShares`.

hypotheses.title: retrieveTokensForWithdraw allows over-retrieval beyond needed assets
hypotheses.description: The function accumulates `amountAskedForWithdraw_temp` from `retrieveData[i].withdrawAmount` (the requested amount, not the actual received `amount`), then checks `if (amountAskedForWithdraw_temp > neededAssets) revert`. However, `neededAssets` is computed once at the start via `neededAssetsForWithdraw()`, which depends on `baseToken.balanceOf(address(this))`. As tokens are retrieved in the loop, the actual balance increases, but `neededAssets` is not recomputed. More importantly, the check uses `retrieveData[i].withdrawAmount` (user-supplied) rather than the actual `amount` returned by the connector. A malicious or buggy connector could return less than requested, yet `amountAskedForWithdraw_temp` still counts the full requested amount, allowing the loop to pass the check while actual retrieved funds are insufficient. Conversely, a connector could return more than requested (the `balanceBefore + amount > balanceAfter` check only ensures the balance increased by at least `amount`, not exactly), and the excess is not accounted for.
hypotheses.attackPath: A trusted connector (or a connector that has been added via the broken `onlyVaultMaintainer` modifier) returns a small `amount` while `retrieveData[i].withdrawAmount` is large. `amountAskedForWithdraw_temp` accumulates the large requested amount, passing the `> neededAssets` check, but actual funds retrieved are insufficient. Then `fulfillCurrentWithdrawGroup` sees `amountAskedForWithdraw == totalCBAmount` and marks the group fulfilled, but `availableAssets < totalCBAmount`, so `totalABAmount < totalCBAmount`, and users receive proportionally less.
hypotheses.impact: Withdraw group can be marked fulfilled with insufficient actual assets, causing users to receive less than their calculated withdrawal amounts (loss of funds).
hypotheses.recommendation: Accumulate the actual `amount` returned by the connector instead of `retrieveData[i].withdrawAmount`, and recompute `neededAssets` inside the loop.

hypotheses.title: executeDeposit mints shares before addLiquidity external call
hypotheses.description: `executeDeposit` mints shares to receivers, updates `totalDepositedAmount`, then calls `IConnector(connector).addLiquidity(...)`. The connector's `addLiquidity` calls back into `AccountingManager.sendTokensToTrustedAddress` to pull the base tokens. If the connector is malicious or reenters, it can observe the already-minted shares and updated `totalDepositedAmount` while the base tokens are still in the AccountingManager, allowing it to manipulate `TVL()` (which includes `baseToken.balanceOf(address(this))`) during the callback.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1. Manager calls `executeDeposit`. 2. Shares are minted, `totalDepositedAmount` updated. 3. `addLiquidity` is called; the connector reenters a view function like `TVL()` or `previewDeposit` while the base tokens are still held, inflating TVL. 4. The connector uses this to compute an advantageous rate for a subsequent operation.
hypotheses.impact: TVL manipulation during the callback window can lead to incorrect share pricing for concurrent operations.
hypotheses.recommendation: Transfer base tokens to the connector before minting shares, or add a reentrancy guard that blocks view functions during the callback.

hypotheses.title: Keepers.execute nonce incremented before external call
hypotheses.description: `execute` increments `nonce` before making the external call to `destination`. This is the correct ordering for replay protection, but the external call is made without a reentrancy guard. If `destination` reenters `execute`, the nonce has already been incremented, so the reentrant call uses a new nonce and requires fresh signatures — which the attacker does not have. However, the reentrant call can still execute if the attacker has valid signatures for the new nonce (e.g., from a pending transaction). More importantly, the `emit Execute` happens before the call, so off-chain indexers may record the execution before it succeeds.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1. Attacker obtains valid signatures for nonce N+1 (e.g., from a mempool observation). 2. Attacker triggers `execute` for nonce N, which calls a malicious `destination`. 3. `destination` reenters `execute` with nonce N+1 and the pre-obtained signatures. 4. Both executions succeed, potentially executing unintended transactions.
hypotheses.impact: Reentrant execution of signed transactions, potentially bypassing intended sequencing.
hypotheses.recommendation: Add a `nonReentrant` modifier to `execute`, or move the external call after all state updates and emit.

hypotheses.title: retrieveTokensForWithdraw can be griefed to revert via amountAskedForWithdraw
hypotheses.description: `retrieveTokensForWithdraw()` accumulates `amountAskedForWithdraw` and reverts if `amountAskedForWithdraw_temp > neededAssets`. Because `neededAssetsForWithdraw()` depends on live `baseToken.balanceOf(address(this))` and `depositQueue.totalAWFDeposit`, an attacker can manipulate the vault's base token balance (e.g. by triggering a deposit that increases `totalAWFDeposit`, or by causing a connector to send tokens) so that `neededAssets` shrinks mid-call, making the manager's retrieve call revert. Repeatedly, this can prevent the withdraw group from ever being fulfilled.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker observes an active withdraw group with `totalCBAmount > 0`. 2) Attacker front-runs the manager's `retrieveTokensForWithdraw` with a deposit that increases `depositQueue.totalAWFDeposit`, reducing `neededAssetsForWithdraw()`. 3) Manager's call reverts with `NoyaAccounting_INVALID_AMOUNT`. 4) Withdraw group cannot be fulfilled; users' funds stuck.
hypotheses.impact: Withdraw group fulfillment blocked; user withdrawals frozen.
hypotheses.recommendation: Snapshot `neededAssets` at group start and compare against that, or allow partial fulfillment without reverting.

hypotheses.title: Keepers.execute allows any owner to grief via gasLimit and nonce consumption
hypotheses.description: `execute()` requires `isOwner[msg.sender]` and increments `nonce` before the external call. Any single owner can call `execute()` with a `destination`/`data` that reverts (or with a `gasLimit` too low to succeed), consuming the nonce and reverting the whole tx — but since the nonce increment is inside the same tx, the revert rolls it back. However, an owner can also call `execute()` with valid signatures for a benign tx and a `gasLimit` that causes the inner call to fail, reverting the entire multisig operation and blocking legitimate proposals that share the same nonce. More importantly, since `threshold > 1`, a single malicious owner cannot alone pass, but can repeatedly submit failing txs to waste other owners' signatures (signatures are bound to `nonce`, so a failed tx invalidates collected signatures).
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Malicious owner collects threshold signatures for a legitimate tx at nonce N. 2) Before execution, malicious owner calls `execute()` with the same nonce N but a `destination` that reverts. 3) The tx reverts, but the signatures are now unusable for the intended tx (nonce unchanged but signatures were for the same nonce — actually reusable, but the malicious owner can keep front-running). 4) Legitimate execution is delayed indefinitely.
hypotheses.impact: Multisig operations (including emergency actions) can be indefinitely delayed by a single owner.
hypotheses.recommendation: Use a per-proposal nonce or commit-reveal scheme; do not bind signatures to a global monotonic nonce that any owner can consume.

hypotheses.title: ChainlinkOracleConnector.getValue uses stale/inverse price without validating round completeness
hypotheses.description: `getValueFromChainlinkFeed` reads `latestRoundData()` and checks `block.timestamp - updatedAt > chainlinkPriceAgeThreshold` and `price <= 0`. It does not check `answeredInRound >= roundId` nor that `updatedAt != 0`. If a feed is deprecated or returns a stale round with `updatedAt = 0`, the check `block.timestamp - 0 > threshold` will revert (good). But if `updatedAt` is recent yet the round is incomplete (answeredInRound < roundId), the price may be from a previous round. More importantly, the inverse calculation `(amountIn * sourceTokenUnit) / uintprice` can be manipulated if `uintprice` is small. An attacker cannot directly set the feed, but can exploit a feed with low precision or a token with few decimals.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker finds a token with low decimals and a feed with low precision. 2) Attacker manipulates the underlying market to push the price to an extreme. 3) The inverse calculation amplifies the error, returning a wildly wrong value. 4) Attacker uses this to deposit/withdraw at a favorable rate.
hypotheses.impact: Wrong accounting, theft.
hypotheses.recommendation: Add `answeredInRound >= roundId` and `updatedAt != 0` checks, and bound the inverse calculation.
